title: Inside three.ws: The Open-Source Stack That Gives AI Agents a Body, a Brain, a Wallet, and a Job
gist: three.ws is an Apache-2.0 open-source stack that bundles 3D avatar generation, a multi-model agent runtime with typed memory and a seven-layer guard chain, and an on-chain wallet using the x402 pay-per-call payment standard, distributed via a web component, AR, MCP, ChatGPT, and Android, while carefully distinguishing verified partnerships (OpenAI Select Partner, NVIDIA Inception) from unofficial marketplace listings.

insights.claim: three.ws argues that a real AI agent needs four things bundled into a single product rather than solved separately: a body (a visible, expressive 3D form), a brain (a tool-calling, memory-holding model), a wallet (a way to pay for compute and settle with other agents without a human signing every transaction), and distribution (the ability to exist on a website, chat assistant, phone, or terminal).
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: Signals a bet that vertically-integrated agent infrastructure (body+brain+wallet+distribution) beats point solutions, relevant for anyone evaluating whether narrow agent tooling startups get commoditized by full-stack players.
insights.quote: three.ws is the argument that these are one product.
insights.locator: The thesis: an agent needs four things, and they belong in one stack

insights.claim: three.ws's Forge tool does not rely on a single 3D generation model; it runs a registry of engines (Microsoft TRELLIS, Tencent Hunyuan3D 2.1/2, TripoSR, TripoSG-scribble) with live health checks and 'free-first routing,' sending each request down the cheapest healthy lane and automatically failing over to the next lane when one is rate-limited or down.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: A multi-model failover router insulates the product from any single model vendor's downtime or rate limits, a pattern worth tracking as a template for other AI-infra products managing vendor risk and cost.
insights.locator: Generation is a routing problem

insights.claim: On the free generation tier, three.ws works around a model limitation by silently appending 'studio lighting' to prompts because the free TRELLIS lane truncates prompts at 77 characters and defaults to dark output, and it pins sampling steps at 15/15 for the free lane versus 40/40 reserved for the self-hosted TRELLIS worker to fit within a synchronous response window.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: Shows how thin the margin is on 'free' AI generation products -- providers quietly trade quality (fewer sampling steps, prompt patching) for cost control, a pattern relevant to modeling unit economics of any freemium generative-AI service.
insights.locator: Two details that matter more than they sound

insights.claim: three.ws's photo-to-avatar pipeline reconstructs a rigged face in about five seconds on CPU alone (no GPU required) using MediaPipe FaceLandmarker and a fixed-topology template, and quality is enforced by an automated, texture-blind 'Identity Shape Error' metric plus a weekly benchmark that renders 23 fixed prompts against reference photos and scores them with Gemini vision on Vertex AI, rather than manual human review.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: A CPU-only, automatically-graded fidelity pipeline suggests a materially lower per-generation compute cost than GPU-bound competitors, and an automated eval loop is a reusable pattern for scaling quality control on generative pipelines.
insights.locator: The selfie lane

themes.theme: Rig-agnostic animation as a technical moat

insights.claim: Instead of restricting itself to an allowlist of supported rig formats, three.ws's retargeting engine (built on the MIT-licensed Make-It-Animatable) canonicalizes roughly twenty different bone-naming conventions from tools like Blender, VRoid, Daz, Reallusion, Mixamo, and Roblox onto one 52-bone skeleton, so a model can be animated with as few as 8 matching canonical bones and a rig that truly cannot be driven falls back to a default body rather than freezing.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: Interoperability across the entire existing universe of 3D avatar assets (rather than requiring re-creation in a proprietary format) removes a major adoption barrier for a 3D-avatar platform and is a defensible technical bar for competitors to match.
insights.locator: Rigging any mesh, and the end of the rig allowlist

insights.claim: three.ws's shared motion-capture library holds about 3,000 clips, with a full clip carrying 53 tracks (52 bone rotations plus hip position) of which 30 tracks address finger joints specifically, and the platform also supports text-to-motion generation via the Motion Diffusion Model, video-to-motion via MediaPipe pose/hand tracking solved with an in-house NumPy inverse-kinematics solver (no GPU needed), and continuous sign-language synthesis and recognition.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: Multi-modal motion generation (text, video, and webcam capture, all GPU-free for the video path) broadens the addressable use cases beyond simple avatar demos toward accessibility tools like sign-language translation.
insights.locator: The motion library and where motion comes from

insights.claim: Every post-generation processing stage on three.ws (rig, remesh, stylize, background removal) is independently priced as a micropayment 'x402' resource with no account required -- for example rig costs $0.05 and background removal $0.01 -- and a stage whose underlying worker is unconfigured returns an error before any payment settles, so failed stages are never charged.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: Demonstrates a working implementation of granular, per-API-call micropayments for AI services -- a business model investors are watching as a potential alternative to subscription pricing for agentic/API-consumed AI products.
insights.locator: Every stage is also an x402 resource with no key and no account

insights.claim: As of 25 August 2026, three.ws's self-hosted x402 payment facilitator reports 110,416 on-chain USDC settlements and 803,483 payment verifications across a live discovery catalog of 4,519 priced endpoints.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, checkable transaction-volume baseline for a live agent-payments rail, useful as a reference point for tracking growth or stagnation in machine-to-machine stablecoin payments.
insights.locator: The numbers, from the platform's self-hosted facilitator as of 25 August 2026

insights.claim: three.ws anchors agent identity on Solana (via a Metaplex Core on-chain asset and SPL Memo attestations, alongside the platform's $THREE token) while also deploying ERC-8004 identity, reputation, and validation registries via CREATE2 to the same contract address across twelve EVM mainnets, using a delegated-signer pattern so the wallet owner's cold key never has to be online for the agent to transact.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: A dual-chain identity design (Solana-native plus cross-EVM ERC-8004) with cold-key isolation is a concrete architecture pattern for autonomous agent custody risk that other agent-wallet projects will likely be compared against.
insights.locator: Identity

insights.claim: three.ws explicitly reports that its 'agent-economy volume' page -- the total USDC actually moved between agents hiring each other on the marketplace -- has no sample or placeholder data path, so if the true completed-hire volume is zero the page states zero rather than showing a fabricated number.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: A candid admission that agent-to-agent hiring volume can be zero suggests the agent-to-agent marketplace layer (distinct from the human-to-agent payment rail) is still pre-traction, a useful caveat against over-reading the platform's other usage numbers as proof of a live agent economy.
insights.quote: There is no sample data path in that page. When the number is zero, it says so.
insights.locator: The agent wallet and the agent economy

themes.theme: Agent brain, memory, and financial guardrails

insights.claim: three.ws's agent 'brain' is architected as a router rather than a single model, fanning each prompt across a wide multi-vendor roster (Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT-5.x/o3, xAI Grok, Groq-hosted Llama 3.3, Alibaba Qwen, DeepSeek R1, IBM Granite, and a free NVIDIA NIM model garden) with a deterministic failover order -- native provider, then a mirrored OpenRouter id, then Groq, then OpenRouter's free tier, then NIM -- so that an agent never goes silent because a single vendor has an outage.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: A deterministic multi-vendor LLM failover chain reduces dependence on any one foundation-model provider's uptime and pricing, a defensive architecture pattern investors should expect to see replicated across agent-infrastructure products.
insights.locator: The brain

insights.claim: three.ws agents use typed memory split into four categories (user, feedback, project, reference) that carry different salience bonuses, are ranked by salience times a recency boost with a seven-day half-life, and are injected into the system prompt inside a strict 8,192-token budget, pruned once memory exceeds 150 entries.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: A concrete, bounded memory-ranking scheme (rather than unlimited context stuffing) is a scalable pattern for managing long-running agent context costs, relevant to anyone assessing token-cost efficiency of persistent-memory agent products.
insights.locator: The tool loop, memory, and emotion

insights.claim: Every fund-moving tool call an agent makes on three.ws passes through seven independent enforcement layers that always all run in full (security blacklist, human intervention, capability, permission, trade guard, spend envelope, x402 budget), producing an allow / require_approval / block verdict, and if any single guard layer fails to execute that failure is itself surfaced as a finding rather than silently ignored.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: This 'defense in depth plus fail-loud' design for autonomous agent spending is a benchmark risk-control pattern investors and enterprises evaluating agentic-payment safety should look for -- or ask why it is absent -- in competing agent-wallet products.
insights.quote: A guard that failed to run is reported as a finding, not silently skipped.
insights.locator: The guard chain: autonomy with a seatbelt

insights.claim: three.ws packages its avatars as a single lazy-loading web component (<agent-3d>) embeddable on any site, and extends the same generation logic to AR placement (iOS Quick Look, Android Scene Viewer, WebXR), a hosted MCP server usable from Claude Desktop and Cursor, a live custom GPT in the OpenAI GPT Store, a signed Android app with Solana Seed Vault wallet integration, and even a terminal renderer (npx @three-ws/tty-avatar).
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: Breadth of distribution surfaces (web, AR, chat assistants, mobile, terminal) from one generation backend lowers the marginal cost of reaching new user channels, a scale advantage worth weighing against narrower single-surface competitors.
insights.locator: Distribution: existing everywhere

insights.claim: 72 three.ws MCP servers are listed under one namespace in the official Model Context Protocol registry, and the company released 'Spatial MCP' under a CC0 license as a proposed response-shape standard so that a 3D scene can be returned as a native MCP result rather than just a URL pasted into text.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: Publishing an open, CC0-licensed spatial data spec is an attempt to set a de facto interoperability standard for 3D content inside the MCP ecosystem -- worth watching for adoption by other MCP tool builders as a sign three.ws is shaping, not just using, the protocol.
insights.locator: MCP: assistants call the same tools

insights.claim: three.ws explicitly separates two partner-granted statuses -- OpenAI Select Partner (accepted 14 July 2026) and NVIDIA Inception member (accepted July 2026) -- from a longer list of marketplace listings, startup-program memberships, and directory placements, stating outright that none of the latter category is an endorsement.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: This is an unusually granular partnership-credibility disclosure for a promotional post; investors evaluating any AI startup's claimed 'partnerships' should look for this kind of tiering rather than taking a logo wall at face value.
insights.quote: We would rather you trust the list than be impressed by it.
insights.locator: Partners and programs

insights.claim: Despite the IBM relationship already being covered by Yahoo Finance and Business Insider Markets and having its own IBM Community user group, three.ws states plainly that its public Granite-model integrations are independent developer tools built on IBM's publicly available models rather than IBM products, and that the formal partnership work is not yet public.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: A caution against reading media coverage of a partnership as proof of a finalized commercial relationship -- the underlying legal/commercial partnership can lag well behind the press narrative, relevant to due diligence on any startup's announced enterprise tie-ups.
insights.quote: the formal partnership work is not yet public
insights.locator: IBM

insights.claim: three.ws's native token $THREE is Jupiter Verified and Phantom Verified and is listed on MEXC, LBank, KCEX, Bybit Alpha, KuCoin Alpha, Binance Web3, Coinbase Wallet, CoinGecko, and CoinMarketCap.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: Broad secondary-market listing for the platform's native token gives it real, liquid tradability well beyond a typical pre-revenue dev-tool startup, a relevant data point for anyone tracking crypto-AI convergence plays.
insights.locator: Exchanges, listings, and market data

insights.claim: three.ws frames Hugging Face publication as a way to let outside observers cheaply verify its marketing claims by opening the actual rigged glTF files rather than trusting a description, and backs this with a live production version endpoint (GET https://three.ws/api/version) that reveals the exact commit hash currently running in production.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: Publishing verifiable, checkable artifacts (open weights, open code, a live version endpoint) rather than closed demos is a credibility-building tactic that reduces due-diligence friction for investors and enterprise partners evaluating the claims.
insights.locator: Why this belongs on Hugging Face

insights.claim: As of 25 August 2026, three.ws's Apache-2.0 open-source ecosystem spans 101 npm packages (42 of them MCP servers), 72 registered MCP servers, 33 GPU/CPU workers, seven Solidity contracts, two Solana programs, 60 agent skills, roughly 1,750 test files, and over 500 CC0 3D props plus 106 rigged characters and 3,000+ mocap animations released as open assets.
insights.speaker: three.ws
insights.so_what: A large, itemized open-source surface area (rather than a single flagship repo) suggests meaningful engineering investment and gives investors concrete metrics to track for growth or stagnation over time.
insights.locator: Open source, in numbers
